content.title: General Response
content.comment:
We want to express sincere appreciation for all reviewers' efforts in reviewing and providing valuable suggestions! We have tried to address reviewers' major concerns respectively.  

We understand that the major common concern of reviewers comes from novelty. We would like to elaborate on the novelty of our work as follows.

Our novelty lies in two aspects: a new perspective of non-autoregressive sequence modeling via underlying dynamical systems, and from such a perspective we choose the deep equilibrium network (DEQ) as one of the right tools for the purpose of solving the stationary state of such a dynamical system.

Both of them are non-trivial.
- First, **the major contribution of the proposed dynamical system view of NAR sequence model is that it offers a more principled and unified way for future research in NAR sequence modeling, regarding both explicit iterative refinement and implicit ones**. For example, the perspective of dynamical systems of NAR sequence modeling enables the potential of the recent advances of neural ODEs or other promising dynamical system-inspired generative models such as denoising diffusion probabilistic model and score-based generative SDEs.
- Second, **as we have already discussed in the Section 3.4 in our original submission, the use of DEQ to solve the dynamical system of NAR sequence modeling is not straightforward and yet unexplored**. To highlight, 
  - (1) the DEQ network proposed in the original paper was for unconditional autoregressive language modeling, whilst in this paper, DEQNAR aims at non-autoregressive models 
  - (2) the original DEQ network was applied for position by position, whereas DEQNAR models a dynamical system where the whole sequence evolves layer-wisely. As a result, these fundamental differences necessitate considerable effort to solve all the related research problems. 
  - (3) the original DEQ paper only studied the dynamic evolving in feature/representation level, whereas our work comprehensively studies not only continuous feature state space, but also covers discrete state space and the mix of the both, which have never been studied and known before for DEQ framework. 

We again thank everyone's time and effort in discussing, providing valuable and inspiring feedback, and helping us improve our manuscript. We do sincerely appreciate you!

Many thanks, and cheers!

Authors

content.title: Response to Reviewer 6M3x
content.comment:
Thanks very much for your insightful comments! We would like to address your major concerns below.

$$$$

**Q1**: The methodology and model formulation is very similar to the DEQ sequence model proposed by Bai, 2019, which is also mentioned by the author. The author tries to explain the difference of their work with DEQ in a short paragraph before section 4, but I still failed to see the major differences. Since this is crucial for judging the novelty of this work, I strongly suggest the author should elaborate on the differences, especially during the modelling stage, instead of postponing everything in the end stage.

**A1**: Thanks for pointing out your concerns about novelty. Please refer to our general response. And thanks for your suggestion for improving presenation, which is very useful. We will make necessary changes accordingly in our next version. Thank you!

$$$$

**Q2**: Also for section 3.2, can the non-differentiability with the sampling operator be solved by using Gumble-softmax trick?

**A2**: We in fact provided explicit options such as Gumbel softmax as you mentioned (Appendix C & Table 5). We found that, to our surprise, gumbel softmax performed terribly and even failed to train.  We hypothesize that it may be caused by the family of Newton's methods' significant difficulties in scaling to extremely sparse and high-dimensional space (i.e., probability simplex, whose dimension is the vocabulary size |V| >> hidden dimension of NNs).

$$$$

**Q3**: Questions for clarity, missing references, and suggestions for presentation problems

**A3**: We are really grateful for your suggestions. As a result, we will include them to enhance our next version. Many thanks!

content.title: Response to Reviewer DdDk
content.comment:
Thanks very much for your insightful comments! We would like to address your major concerns below.

$$$$

**Q1**: Limited novelty as it seems more like an application of DEQs to NAR models

**A1**: We appreciate you raising the concerns about novelty. Please refer to our general response. 

$$$$

**Q2**: Scaling properties have not been studied, i.e., how much do we gain in performance/resource trade-off by increasing the number of evaluations required to achieve equilibrium

**A2**: Thanks for your suggestion. We actually have provided relevant discussion in Figure 1(c), where we indeed find that our model saturates at around 10 steps of iteration, and we also found strong correlation between accuracy and convergence statbility in Figure 3.  Besides, we also pointed out the potential accuracy-efficiency trade-off in Section 4.2. We will revise our manuscript to be clearer to prevent any further confusion on this. Thank you!

$$$$

**Q3**: Training Time: Is there a comparison of the training time of baseline architecture and the proposed framework?

**A3**: Yes. In fact, we have provided such results and discussion in Section 4.2 and Figure 4. 

$$$$

**Q4**: GLAT + CTC: Why is it the case that GLAT+CTC baseline in Table 3 has ≈16.8x speed up as compared to only 4.2x speed up with DEQNAR? Does it mean that there's no speed benefits? Even the performance is somewhat comparable ( 27.20 vs 26.9 ).

**A4**: The additional NFEs for DEQNAR (20 vs. 6 for GLAT+CTC) are what cause the computational overhead. On one hand, when compared to implicit/fully NAR approaches, our method often requires more NEFs. On the other hand, we can tell from Table 3 that our method could somewhat be a little bit more efficient than most explicit iterative methods (when trained on Transformer-big KD data as similar to other explicit iterative methods). 

$$$$

**Q5**: Questions for clarity, missing references, and suggestions for presentation problems

**A5**: We are really grateful for your suggestions. As a result, we will include them to enhance our next version. Many thanks!

content.title: Response to Reviewer MjXd
content.comment:
Thanks very much for your insightful comments! We would like to address your major concerns below.

$$$$

**Q1**: Novelty concerns. Everything in this paper was known before and there isn't much contribution on the methodology end (other than the good BLEU scores). For example, DEQ, NA-NMT with deep supervision, inexact gradient, convergence analysis, etc. are all known before. In a certain sense, the method that is applied in this work seems to be not much different from DEQ models applied to image classification (which is clearly also non-autoregressive). And there were no "explicit challenges" in combining them.

**A1**: We appreciate you raising the concerns about novelty. Please refer to our general response. 

Additionally, despite the fact that models for image classification are typically non-autoregressive, they are discriminate models and only necessarily involve one categorical output variable to be determined given data. While determining structured, inter-dependent, and multi-variate output data is necessary for sequence generative modeling, it is substantially more difficult from a modeling perspective than typical classification tasks. Because of this, even though DEQ is successful in image classiﬁcation, it is not straightforward to expect that DEQ framework could address the problem of sequence production without "explicit challenges," such as deliberate task-specific exploration and adaptation.

$$$$

**Q2**:  The paper is titled "non-autoregressive sequence learning" and yet only evaluates NMT tasks. Why not just say non-autoregressive NMT? 

**A2**: Thanks for your suggestion. We initially thought that sequence generation was best represented by the machine translation task. To improve our study, we will take your advice and add more tasks (e.g., as summarization) in the future revision.

$$$$

**Q3**. The authors propose a "softmax relaxation" for the explicit iterative refinement, which, in my opinion, no longer seems "explicit". I wonder if the authors have considered some explicit options that are differentiable as well, such as a Gumbel softmax layer in the iterative layer?

**A3**: We in fact provided explicit options such as Gumbel softmax as you mentioned (Appendix C & Table 5). We found that, to our surprise, gumbel softmax performed terribly and even failed to train.  We hypothesize that it may be caused by the family of Newton's methods' significant difficulties in scaling to extremely sparse and high-dimensional space (i.e., probability simplex, whose dimension is the vocabulary size |V| >> hidden dimension of NNs).

$$$$

**Q4**: Questions for clarity and suggestions for presentation problems

**A4**: We are really grateful for your suggestions. We will accordingly include them to enhance our next version. Many thanks!

Thanks very much for your insightful comments! We would like to address your major concerns below.

$$$$

**Q1**: Results are not so clear cut, sometimes inconsistent or confusing. No uncertainty estimators, some numbers are missing.

**A1**: Sorry for confusing. Actually, our experiments were initially implemented and conducted upon official Fairseq. Afterward we discovered that the recently opensourced Fully-NAT codebase of [1] has better GLAT+CTC and VAE+CTC implementation and decided to change our codebase accordingly. Due to the impending submission deadline, we were only able to re-run some new experiments regarding GLAT+CTC and VAE+CTC and updated Figure 2, while mistakenly misusing some old numbers in Table 3, creating such inconsistency and confusion. 

The next version will be accurate and more understandable. We appreciate you bringing this up.

$$$$


**Q2**: Novelty. Unclear how much of the contribution is the proposed architecture, or the stability improvements to make it train on this problem.

**A2**: We appreciate you raising the concerns about novelty. Please refer to our general response. 

$$$$


**Q3**: Questions for clarity and suggestions for presentation problems

**A3**: We are really grateful for your suggestions. We will accordingly include them to enhance our next version. Many thanks!

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper explores the space of non-autoregressive architectures (NAR) for modeling token sequences, in which the probability of sampling each token is independent from the other tokens sampled (given the penultimate layer). Such models typically proceed by iterative refinement, where the same trainable function (e.g., one or more transformer layers, with or without a discretization step) is applied in a recurrent manner a given number of times.
It introduces a deep equilibrium view of that iterative process, DeqNAR, proposing to replace it with a fixed-point process, which can be solved by black-box solvers, and trained by gradient descent by differentiating through the fixed point.
This model is compatible with various recent techniques for NARs (VAE models, CTC objective, GLAT training strategy). Numerous experimental evaluations show it compares favorably to regular iterative refinement techniques on languages translation benchmarks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
---------------
1. Interesting application of DEQ training of transformer layers, for non-autoregressive sequence prediction.
2. Extensive comparisons against published baselines, showing the method is applicable in different settings.

Weaknesses
------------------
1. Results are not so clear cut, sometimes inconsistent or confusing. No uncertainty estimators, some numers are missing.
2. Unclear how much of the contribution is the proposed architecture, or the stability improvements to make it train on this problem.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity
---------
The paper's structure is clear, the content is understandable and fairly well explained. Some things could be better explained, see suggestions and questions below.

Suggestions:
1. Figure 5 is referred to several times in the main text, so it should be in the main paper and not the appendix.
2. The points of Fig 4 and 5 may be made more easily if they were plotted against wall-clock time, rather than steps

Questions:
1. Table 1, why should the "explicit" variant have more transformer layers than the others? Is it just a modeling choice, the thing that worked better experimentally, or a fundamental difference?
2. Table 1, are all the $\mathcal F$ the same?
3. I did not understand the role of the "Dirac delta distribution", does it just say that $\boldsymbol{z_t} = \boldsymbol{\mu} = \mathcal{F}(\boldsymbol{z}_{t-1})$?
4. Sec. 3.3, does the definition of the fusion operator $\sigma$ imply that $d = |\mathcal{V}|$? Could it be more general, so that $d$ is larger?
5. Tables 2 and 3: what are the bolded numbers?
6. In Fig. 3, is each dot a single example (sentence pair)? From the test split?
7. A.2, is the final objective used for both implicit and explicit versions of the model? Are the hyperparameters the same?

Inconsistencies, small issues or typos:
1. p2, "is almost indeed via"?
2. Table 1, is there a difference between $f$ (first row) and $\mathcal F$ (rows 2 and 3)?
3. Sec. 4.1, DeqNAR-LP is mentioned, but never introduced or mentioned again.
4. Sec. 4.1, missing ")" after "Appendix C"
5. Sec. 4.1 "interior performance" -> "inferior"?
6. Table 3, should "Transformer-_big_ KD" be prefixed by a "*"?
7. Sec. 4.2, "we can infer from Figure 3 that DeqNAR achieves" should it be "Figure 4"?
8. B. 3, leading ". ".
9. C. 1, p.16: What is DeqNAR-mixed**?
10. Table 5, "logtis" -> "logits"?
11. Fig. 6, extra ")" in caption
12. C. 2 (1) should there be an "=" sign in the formula at the bottom of p. 17?

Quality
----------
The range of experiments performed, including the baselines, is appropriate for a practical contribution of this nature.
They show in practice that this modeling is compatible with different kinds of variants of NAR methods (models, objectives, training).
Reporting experiments with negative results (for explicit refinement) in App C 1 is a good thing, that should be encouraged.

However, some of the results do not seem strong enough to support the claims made. For instance:
1. "explicit iterative refinement is among the currently strongest NAR systems": why not take that one as a baseline, then?
2. "we find that DeqNAR-mixed takes advantages of both implicit and explicit refinement": what's the evidence for this? The improvement is minor, and may be due to increased capacity, or something else.
3. baseline numbers (and some of the DeqNAR numbers) do not always match between Figure 2 and Table 3, for what looks like the same model.
4. In particular, DeqNAR seems to beat Gu & Kong (2021) on Fig. 2, but that's not the case any more in Table 3.
5. some numbers are missing from Table 3.
6. Sec. 4.2, "such manner of convergence of DeqNAR is the reason behind its superior performance [...] the DEQ-based model becomes more accurate when it gets closer to its equilibrium". In Figure 3, could it just be that "easy" examples converge faster than "harder" examples? In that case, the speed of convergence would just reflect the complexity of the data, rather than the quality of the model.
7. Figures 2, 4, 5, as well as Table 3 should have confidence intervals to show uncertainty. I suspect some models may be statistically tied.

Novelty
----------
Despite the paragraph at the end of Sec 3.4, it is not clear to me how much the novelty of the contribution is
1. a novel formulation of the NAR methods, inserting the DEQ methodology to a new architecture, or
2. a collection of stabilization tricks, mostly described in Appendix A, that enable scaling the DEQ-Transformer (Bai et al. 2019) to a higher-dimensional problem with a particular structure.

Reproducibility
--------------------
The methods are defined clearly enough that the methods could be implemented by someone familiar with the fields. Reproducing the experimental results, however, seems more tricky, especially since no source code is provided, nor promised to open source.

In particular, there is missing information regarding:
1. Which fusion operator $\sigma$ is used
2. hyperparameters of the solver (Anderson optimization)
3. values of hyperparameters for the architecture chosen ($d$...)
4. values of the hyperparameters defined in A.2 ($\lambda_\mathrm{corr}$, $\lambda_\mathrm{init}$), whether they are the same for all experiments or not, or how they were chosen / validated

In general there seems to be quite a bit of subtlety in stabilizing the convergence, and it seems tricky to reproduce. In fact, the difference in some numbers reported in Fig 2 and  Table 3 suggests reproducing exact results is hard.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The presented technique seems interesting, and could be useful for non-autoregressive symbolic sequence prediction tasks.
A comparison showing the compatibility with an array of existing techniques is promising, but seems still preliminary: missing numbers, no confidence intervals or significance comparison.
Moreover, it's not clear how much of the contribution is a novel formulation of the NAR problem, vs. practical techniques enabling scaling up of existing DEQ-Transformer models.

I'm leaning towards not accepting the paper as not ready yet, but there's ample space for clarifications and improvements.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes to integrate deep equilibrium (DEQ) models with non-autoregressive NMT (NA-NMT) by leveraging the iterative nature of the latter. The authors argue that the iterative refinement process seen in SOTA non-autoregressive NMT models make these models inherently suitable for the implicit deep learning framework, and that by using a DEQNAR model we can have better results while using less computation budget.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**:
1) The paper is well-motivated. Neither implicit DL nor NA-NMT is new and yet to the best knowledge of the reviewer there is no existing exploration on how they can be integrated.
2) BLEU score results are strong. The paper show improvement in a pretty model-agnostic way that DEQNAR can complement many existing non-autoregressive NMT models.
3) The writing is generally clear.

**Weaknesses**:
1) Overall, I find this paper a bit "un-interesting", specifically:
    i) Everything in this paper was known before and there isn't much contribution on the methodology end (other than the good BLEU scores). For example, DEQ, NA-NMT with deep supervision, inexact gradient, convergence analysis, etc. are all known before. In a certain sense, the method that is applied in this work seems to be not much different from DEQ models applied to image classification (which is clearly also non-autoregressive) [1].
    ii) The paper is titled "non-autoregressive sequence learning" and yet only evaluates NMT tasks. Why not just say non-autoregressive NMT? Otherwise, tasks like text summarization and (non-streaming) speech recognition should also fall into this category.
    iii) For the convergence analysis the authors compared mainly using GLAT. Yet it is more interesting to compare DEQ with CTC+DSLP where deep supervision is explicitly used in an NA-NMT model. I suspect that unlike GLAT in Fig. 1(c), a DSLP model should converge better due to its deep supervision. Moreover, as [2] demonstrated, the first few iterations seem most crucial for NA-NMT models in order to avoid multi-modality problem. I think to analyze convergence, the ablations and analysis (e.g., seq_len vs iterations) presented in [2] may be a good reference for the authors. I'm not fully convinced by the author's assumption on why an infinite-depth Transformer is necessary (see Sec. 3.1).
2) The authors propose a "softmax relaxation" for the explicit iterative refinement, which, in my opinion, no longer seems "explicit". I wonder if the authors have considered some explicit options that are differentiable as well, such as a Gumbel softmax layer in the iterative layer?
3) In Sec. 4.2 the authors claim "Given the same decoding time budget, we can infer from Figure 3..." And yet I cannot tell this conclusion from Fig. 3. To really compare the decoding time budget, I suggest that a BLEU vs. wall-clock-time figure be provided.
4) There are clearly more limitations to the method than those highlighted in Sec. 6. The current limitations in Sec. 6 are not exactly the limitations of the proposed approach, but of many NA-NMT models, and are related to the multi-modality problem in NMT. For DEQNAR, I think it'd be good to provide more context on limitations like decoding time slowdown, convergence instability,  etc.
5) The authors may want to cite [3] as well for the inexact gradient.


[1] https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.08656
[2] https://aclanthology.org/D19-1633.pdf
[3] https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.12803
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
1. The paper is overall clear and the method is well-explained. The motivation of the approach in this setting is very straightforward. In addition, to the best knowledge of the reviewer, there is no prior attempt on combining equilibrium models with NMT.
2. My major concern is the limited novelty of this work. Neither the method (fixed-point solving, inexact gradient, etc.) nor its application in non-autoregressive NMT is new, and there were no "explicit challenges" in combining both.
content.summary_of_the_review: This work has nice empirical results and gives a great preliminary exploration of how recent progress in implicit deep learning could potentially improve the results of non-autoregressive NMT's iterative refinement process. The authors show that with black-box root-solving methods we can directly approach an equilibrium state target language sentence and that DEQNAR is compatible with a lot of prior approaches. However, I found there is a limited technical novelty to the approach, and the authors' analysis of convergence and limitations is a bit lacking.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This work studies the Non-Autoregressive (NAR) sequence learning problem. It reformulates the sequence generation problem as solving the equilibrium state of the dynamical system representing the NAR models.

An NAR system is defined as the dynamical system $z_{t+1} = f_\theta ( z_t, x )$ where $x$ is the input sequence, $f_{\theta}$ is the transition kernel that updates $z_t$ the predicted target representation at time $t$ to the new target sequence representation $z_{t+1}$. If the hidden state $z_t$ are discrete representation of the target sequence, it is referred to as the iterative NAR problem. Whenever the hidden state is a continuous representation, its a fully NAR model.

This work proposes DEQNAR, a framework that finds the equilibrium state of NAR models. It has the following desirable properties: 
- $z^* = f_{\theta}( z^*, x )$ is the fixed point/ equilibrium solution to the NAR model. Thus eliminating the naive iterative layer stacking.
- Better convergence to equilibrium due to access to advanced solvers such as quasi-Newton methods.
- It can be integrated in other advanced training techniques such as better modelling, training objectives, and training strategies, etc.

Empirical evaluations on machine translation tasks on WMT14 English-German and WMT16 English-Romanian datasets shows its effectiveness.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths: 
- Models a dynamical system for NAR models and provides a working framework DEQNAR that achieve equilibrium solutions 
- It can be easily integrated with other NAR training techniques 

Weaknesses:
- Limited novelty as it seems more like an application of DEQs to NAR models
- Performance gains shown on WMT datasets are not impressive as compared to the baselines (see below). 
- Scaling properties have not been studied, i.e., how much do we gain in performance/resource trade-off by increasing the number of evaluations required to achieve equilibrium
- Resource usage has not been clearly defined ( train/inference time/storage comparison )


Questions for Authors:


- Scaling Properties: Can you plot the scaling properties of the DEQNAR? Basically, increasing the number of evaluations from the smallest to the largest possible and show how the performance scales? Does it saturate early with small number of function evaluations? If there's a big jump in performance as the system reaches equilibrium, it would be a compelling argument that you can adaptively trade-off performance for fast inference. 

- Training Time: Is there a comparison of the training time of baseline architecture and the proposed framework? 

- Inference Time: Can you show the inference times of various baselines that achieve similar performance? It is unclear if the speed up translates exactly into the inference speed.

- Storage Overhead: Can you show the parameter counts of the various baselines? It seems some baselines have different parameters ( 65M, 44M, 64M, etc. in Table~5 )

- GLAT + CTC: Why is it the case that GLAT+CTC baseline in Table 3 has $\approx 16.8x$ speed up as compared to only $4.2x$ speed up with DEQNAR? Does it mean that there's no speed benefits? Even the performance is somewhat comparable ( 27.20 vs 26.9 ).

- Transformer-Big acheives 29.20 on EN-DE while best DEQNAR (transformer-big) still is close to 27.51. How do you justify this drop in performance? 


- Do you have any experiments that show comparison (performance, inference/training time) with discretized solvers vs black box solvers? Issue with black-box solvers is that they would require different amount of steps for different inputs. Thus, in a single batch, some target sequences will be generated early while others would be generated a bit late. Besides, the paper has not shown that the performance improves drastically if you reach exact equilibrium. It might be computationally beneficial if the system only achieves an approximate solution to the dynamical system. For instance, some works have shown that DEQ comes with significant computational overhead as compared to simple discretize-and-optimize framework ( https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2022/papers/Kag_Condensing_CNNs_With_Partial_Differential_Equations_CVPR_2022_paper.pdf )
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Novelty of the work is somewhat limited as it seems more like an application of the Deep Equilibrium models in this setting. 

Missing references
      Continuous Time RNN (by Rosenblatt),
	Incremental RNNs (https://openreview.net/forum?id=HylpqA4FwS), 
	Antisymmetric RNN : https://openreview.net/forum?id=ryxepo0cFX

	CoRNN : https://arxiv.org/pdf/2010.00951.pdf
      Time Adaptive RNNs (https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2021/papers/Kag_Time_Adaptive_Recurrent_Neural_Network_CVPR_2021_paper.pdf)
content.summary_of_the_review: This work introduces dynamical systems perspective in Non-Autoregressive modelling. Their proposed framework DEQNAR generated sequences by solving for equilibrium state of an ODE. Their choice of dynamical system is not novel. It comes with other overheads such as training/inference times as compared to other baselines. In addition, the empirical evaluations do not show any significant gains as compared to the baselines.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The author proposes a unified view of NAR model using the deep equilibrium sequence model (DEQ), where the underlying dynamic transition can be viewed as a naive root-finding algorithm for the equilibrium state. Specifically, the author reformulates two variants of NAR: (1) implicit refinement; and (2) explicit refinement under DEQ and proposes a mix of these two models. To train the model, the author uses implicit differentiation to obtain the necessary gradient of the equilibrium state and update the parameters.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Strength
The main logic of the paper is clearly written and easy to understand. But I still find some parts confusing, which I will elaborate in the following. Empirically, the author performs experiments to demonstrate the effectiveness of the DeqNAR compared to the vanilla NAR model. It is also interesting to see some ablation studies regarding the properties of DEQ itself. 

## Weakness

The methodology and model formulation is very similar to the DEQ sequence model proposed by Bai, 2019, which is also mentioned by the author. The author tries to explain the difference of their work with DEQ in a short paragraph before section 4, but I still failed to see the major differences. Since this is crucial for judging the novelty of this work, I strongly suggest the author should elaborate on the differences, especially during the modelling stage, instead of postponing everything in the end stage. 

In addition, you mentioned that, unlike DeqNAR, DEQ-Transformer could not evolve all word states simultaneously. I wonder what are the changes you made so that DeqNAR can evolve all word states? It is better to use equations to explain compared to words.

Also for section 3.2, can the non-differentiability with the sampling operator be solved by using Gumble-softmax trick? Also, should you use a different notation $\tilde{z}_t$ in equation (2)?

For the gradient in equation 3, I think you should cite theorem 1 from Bai, 2019, which is a direct application of such theorem.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The main idea is written clearly and is easy to follow. For the unclear part, I have mentioned it in the previous section. In terms of novelty, at the current stage, I cannot judge it since the formulation is very similar to DEQ, and the section in the main paper is not enough to explain the main differences. For now, I made a guess that the main novelty of this paper is (1) casting the NAR model using the language of DEQ and (2) proposing some modifications like the one in equation (2). If that is the case, I do not think this is significantly novel since (1) the similarity of NAR to DEQ is not that difficult to see, and (2) the main methodology is from the DEQ paper.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper proposed a unified view of NAR model by using the language of DEQ. In general, I find the main logic is easy to understand, but I failed to see the main differences compared to DEQ sequence model. Without it, I cannot judge the novelty of this work.

content.title: Deep Equilibrium Non-Autoregressive Sequence Learning
content.abstract: In this work, we argue that non-autoregressive (NAR) sequence generative models can equivalently be regarded as iterative refinement process towards the target sequence, implying an underlying dynamical system of NAR models: $ \mathbf{z} = \mathcal{f}(\mathbf{z}, \mathbf{x}) \rightarrow \mathbf{y}$. In such a way, the optimal prediction of a NAR model should be the equilibrium state of its dynamics if given infinitely many iterations. However, this is infeasible in practice due to limited computational and memory budgets. To this end, we propose DeqNAR to directly solve for the equilibrium state of NAR models based on deep equilibrium networks (Bai et al., 2019) with black-box root-finding solvers and back-propagate through the equilibrium point via implicit differentiation with constant memory. We conduct extensive experiments on four WMT machine translation benchmarks. Our main findings show that DeqNAR can indeed converge to a more accurate prediction and is a general-purpose framework that consistently yields substantial improvement for several strong NAR backbones.
